Wales received an average of just over 375 million pounds a year through the structural funds, and that was on top of the rural development moneys and on top of the agricultural payments. When Ministers say that Wales will not lose a penny, we are entitled to ask which of those streams they are counting, over what period, and measured against what baseline. A commitment to match a single year is not the same as a commitment to match a seven-year programme, and a commitment expressed in cash terms is not the same as a commitment expressed in real terms. Inflation has done a great deal of work for the Treasury over the last two years, and it will do more.

The second question is who decides. The whole architecture of the structural funds in Wales rested on partnership. Local authorities, further education colleges, the third sector and the Welsh Government sat around the same table and agreed priorities that reflected the economic geography of the place, not the electoral geography of a Department in Whitehall. What is now proposed replaces that with a bidding process in which councils compete against one another for pots of money designed and adjudicated in London. I have nothing against competition, but competition costs money. Every bid that fails represents officer time that a hard-pressed authority in the valleys could have spent on delivery.

The third question is duration. Regeneration is a long game. The projects that worked in my constituency worked because promoters could plan over several years and lever in match funding on the strength of that certainty. Annualised funding buys bunting and consultancy reports. It does not buy the skills pipeline or the transport links that a post-industrial economy actually needs, and I would ask the Minister to address that point directly when he responds.

What we secured in the new agreement matters, and I want to be clear with the House about why. Chapter 11 allowed a foreign investor to sue a government directly, before a tribunal sitting outside our courts, when a democratically enacted law reduced the value of that investor's expected profits. Canada was the most sued party under that chapter. We paid out. More importantly, we were chilled. Officials drafting environmental regulations learned to ask not only whether a measure was sound, but whether it would attract a claim. That is not a hypothetical harm. That is a slow erosion of the capacity of an elected Parliament to govern.

The removal of investor-state dispute settlement between Canada and the United States is therefore a genuine gain, and I acknowledge the negotiators who achieved it. But I would caution members against declaring the file closed. We remain party to other agreements that carry similar mechanisms, including the CPTPP, and the same logic that made chapter 11 objectionable applies with equal force there. If the principle is that a foreign corporation should not have rights of action that a Canadian company does not have, then the principle should be applied consistently, not selectively where it happens to be convenient.

On indigenous rights, the general exception that has been included is welcome, but an exception is only as strong as the willingness of a government to invoke it and defend it. First nations have heard promises about consultation before. What they need is a seat at the table when mandates are set, not a briefing after the text is initialled. I would ask the minister to commit today to a standing indigenous advisory mechanism for trade negotiations, with resources attached, so that the next agreement does not require us to relitigate the same ground.

My difficulty is with the way the choice has been presented to this House and to the country, as though there were only two options: the measures before us tonight, or nothing at all.

There is a third path, and it is the one my constituents keep asking me about. It involves putting the effort into the systems that would allow us to live alongside this virus rather than periodically shutting down. Testing that returns a result in hours rather than days. Contact tracing run locally, by public health teams who know their communities, rather than through a national call centre that reaches barely half the contacts it is given. Proper financial support for isolation, because a worker on the minimum wage with no sick pay will not stay at home for ten days, however many times we tell them to, and we should stop pretending otherwise.

I will also say something about the cost side of the ledger, because it is too often treated as if it were merely economic. In my constituency, cancer referrals are down by a third. Mental health services are reporting demand they cannot meet. Children who were already behind are falling further behind, and they are overwhelmingly the poorest children. The Government's own impact assessment barely engages with any of this. If we are to be asked to weigh lives against lives, we are entitled to see both sides of the scale.

I will support the measures tonight, reluctantly, because the immediate risk to the health service is real. But I say to the Minister that this cannot be the pattern of the next twelve months. Each time we do this, compliance falls and trust falls with it.

Let me be clear about what I understand the position to be. Behaviour that would already constitute an offence remains an offence, and the penalties attaching to it are unchanged. What is new is a duty on employers to take reasonable steps to prevent harassment, enforced through the existing employment tribunal route, with an uplift in compensation where the duty has been breached. Nobody goes to prison for failing to write a policy. Nobody goes to prison for an awkward remark at a Christmas party. The people who go to prison are the people who commit sexual offences, and they went to prison before this Bill and will go to prison after it.

I say that because the alternative narrative, that ordinary workplace interaction is being criminalised, does real damage. It makes employers defensive rather than thoughtful. It encourages the tick-box compliance culture that the Minister and I both dislike, where a company buys an online training module, records the completions and considers the matter closed, while the conduct that actually drives people out of the workplace carries on unaddressed.

What I want to see, and what I hope the guidance will deliver, is a focus on the environments where the risk is highest and the protections weakest. Hospitality. Agency work. Night shifts. Places where the workforce is young, turnover is high and the person you would complain to is often the person you would be complaining about. If the balance the Minister describes is to mean anything in practice, that is where it has to be struck.

Second, I have asked the Department to bring forward proposals within eight weeks for a remediation scheme that covers the works to the standard the review identifies, not the standard previously applied. It requires design work, costings, feasibility documentation and often a commissioned report before a single euro is committed. For a large local authority with a dedicated funding unit, that is manageable. For a voluntary committee in a town like Dundrum, it is a very significant undertaking, done in the evenings by people who already give a great deal of their time. When an application of that kind is unsuccessful, the loss is not only the grant. It is the goodwill, and goodwill does not regenerate quickly.

So my ask of the Minister of State is twofold. First, will he ensure that unsuccessful applicants under call one receive detailed written feedback, not a standard letter, so that the work already done can be built upon rather than repeated? Second, will he look at providing seed funding for project development itself, so that the communities with the least capacity are not systematically disadvantaged relative to those who can afford consultants?

I thank him again for his engagement on this. I know his interest in it is genuine, and I look forward to working with him to bring the project to a conclusion.

Nellie McClung and her contemporaries won the vote in Manitoba in 1916. They did not win it because the argument was suddenly found to be persuasive. They won it because they organised, because they were relentless, and because they made it more uncomfortable for the men in power to refuse than to concede. That is worth remembering in a chamber that likes to congratulate itself on progress it inherited rather than earned.

I would also ask us to be honest about the whole of that history. The suffrage movement in this country included voices that argued for the vote on grounds we would now find indefensible, and the franchise they won did not extend to indigenous women for decades afterwards. We do not honour these figures by flattening them into saints. We honour them by finishing the work, and by noticing who is still outside the door.

Who is outside the door today? Women doing care work for wages that do not cover rent. Women in this country's north without access to a midwife or a shelter. Indigenous women and girls whose disappearances produced a national inquiry and a set of calls to justice, most of which remain unimplemented. Women who cannot take a job because there is no child care space, in a country that has been promising a child care system since the Royal Commission reported in 1970.

Mr. Speaker, brains to think, hands to work, hearts to feel, lives to live. Those women asked for their due. We are the ones now in a position to pay it, and I would suggest that we begin with the measures already sitting before this House rather than with another round of commemoration.

I make that point because a number of the concerns raised this afternoon have been framed as though the drafts were settled policy. They are not, and if the consultation is to be meaningful then the Department must be genuinely willing to change them.

That said, I do not think the concerns are misplaced, and I want to put three of them on the record so that they are captured in the responses. The first is the question of the evidential threshold. As drafted, the codes place a good deal of weight on documentary proof at a stage when the people affected are least likely to be able to produce it. The Department knows the population it is dealing with. It should design for the person with the chaotic housing situation and the missing paperwork, not for the model claimant.

The second is the interaction with the appeals process. If a decision maker departs from the code, what is the remedy, and does the code have the status necessary for that departure to be a ground of challenge? The drafting is ambiguous on this and the ambiguity is not accidental.

The third is resourcing. A code is a set of instructions to staff. Instructions that cannot be followed within the time allocated to a case will not be followed. I would like the Department to publish, alongside the final codes, an assessment of the average handling time each provision implies and confirmation that staffing has been adjusted accordingly.

If those three points are addressed in the final version, I think the codes could do real good. If they are not, we will be back here in eighteen months discussing why the outcomes on the ground bear no resemblance to the intentions expressed today.

I do not draw that comparison lightly, and I am not suggesting that what happens at midnight is comparable in its consequences to what happened then. But the mechanism Clark describes seems to me exactly right for our situation. Decisions taken for domestic reasons, each defensible in isolation, accumulating into an outcome that nobody in particular chose and that few would have chosen if presented with it whole.

We have arrived at this point through a sequence of red lines drawn to manage internal party difficulties rather than to secure national advantage. The customs union went because of a conference speech. Regulatory alignment went because of a leadership contest. Each step narrowed the field of the possible, and each was presented to this House as the settled will of the people when in truth it was the settled convenience of the Government.

What is left is a treaty that provides tariff-free trade in goods, which matters to manufacturers, and almost nothing for services, which are eighty per cent of our economy. There is no mutual recognition of professional qualifications. There is no equivalence decision for financial services beyond the temporary. There is nothing meaningful on data adequacy beyond a bridging period. Our touring musicians will discover in the spring what has been done to them.

I shall vote for the Bill tonight, because the alternative before us at this hour is not a better treaty but no treaty, and I will not inflict that on the people I represent. But I want it recorded that voting for a thing under duress is not the same as endorsing it, and that those who brought us to this pass should not mistake tonight's majority for absolution.

I have a good deal of sympathy with the intention behind that amendment, and I hope she will accept that the Government's position is not one of resistance to the principle but of concern about the mechanism.

The difficulty is that the amendment as drafted would create a freestanding obligation sitting outside the deposit protection schemes, which already have adjudication procedures for precisely this dispute. Those schemes require the landlord to evidence a claim, and where the landlord cannot, the money is returned. Layering a further statutory duty on top risks creating two routes with different standards, and where there are two routes there is confusion, and where there is confusion the party with less time and less money loses.

What I think would achieve her objective more reliably is action on the schemes themselves. I can tell the House that we intend to review the adjudication guidance, in particular the treatment of fair wear and tear, which is the source of the great majority of contested deductions and which is currently interpreted with a good deal of variation between schemes. I would also expect scheme operators to publish outcome data broken down by claim type, so that patterns of unjustified deduction become visible rather than remaining a matter of anecdote.

On the wider point about damages for contractual breach, the House should understand that this provision is not a loophole. Without it, a landlord would have no remedy where a tenant caused genuine damage, and the consequence of that would be higher rents for everybody, including the tenants the amendment seeks to protect. The safeguard is that the charge must reflect actual loss, and that is enforceable. I hope on that basis the hon. Member will feel able not to press the amendment.

Madam Speaker, the sector I am speaking about employs tens of thousands of Canadians directly and supports many times that number indirectly, in communities that in many cases have no realistic alternative employer. When we debate this in Ottawa it can sound abstract. In the towns I represent it is the difference between a family staying and a family leaving, and once they leave they do not come back, and the school loses a classroom, and the rink loses a team, and the arc of that decline is very hard to reverse.

The immediate problem is one of certainty. Investment decisions in this industry are made on a horizon of decades, not quarters. What we have offered over the last several years is a regulatory environment in which the rules change between the application and the approval, in which a project can clear every hurdle set for it and then be halted, and in which the timelines published by the government bear no relationship to the timelines experienced by proponents. Capital does not require a friendly government. It requires a predictable one. We have not been predictable.

I want to anticipate the objection, because it will be made. Members opposite will say that the transition is coming and that we should not be building infrastructure for an industry in decline. I would say two things to that. First, the demand is real today and will be real for a long time, and if we do not supply it somebody with lower standards will. Second, the workers in these communities are precisely the workers we will need for whatever comes next. Pipefitters, welders, electricians, heavy equipment operators. You do not build a low-carbon economy without them. Driving them out of the country now and hoping to recruit them back later is not a plan, and the people I represent see through it.

On the substance, I will say that there are genuine problems and I do not minimize them. Processing times in the asylum system are unacceptable. The IRB backlog has grown, and a claimant waiting three years for a hearing is badly served whatever the eventual outcome, as is the public. Housing pressure in the reception system is real, and municipalities have been left to carry costs that are properly federal. Those are legitimate subjects for criticism and I have criticized the government on them myself.

But the answer to a slow system is to resource it, not to redefine who deserves a hearing. Every claim we process quickly and fairly is a decision the public can have confidence in. Every claim that sits for years is an argument handed to those who would prefer we made no determinations at all.

I want to address the argument that has been made about the Convention itself, because it keeps surfacing in these debates and it needs answering. It is said that the ECHR is a foreign imposition, that it has been expanded by judicial interpretation beyond what its drafters intended, and that we should be free of it. Whatever one thinks of that as a proposition, it cannot be advanced honestly while we remain a party. We either denounce the Convention, with all that would mean for the Good Friday agreement, for the trade and cooperation agreement and for our standing in every negotiation we enter, or we comply with it. What we cannot do is remain a signatory while legislating in terms designed to make compliance optional.

The principles at issue here are not exotic. Access to a court. A reasoned decision. Some proportion between what a person has done and what is done to them. These are not obstacles to effective government, they are the conditions under which government commands consent, and I would ask Members on all sides to consider how they would wish these powers to be exercised by a government they did not support.

Once it begins, it does not require oxygen from the air to continue. That is the crucial point, and it is the one that firefighters keep asking us to understand. You cannot smother it. The cell generates its own oxidant as it decomposes, temperatures reach several hundred degrees within seconds, and the fire reignites hours after it appears to have been extinguished.

What that means in a domestic setting is a fire that develops from nothing to untenable conditions in under a minute, frequently in a hallway, because that is where people charge an e-bike, and the hallway is the escape route. The London Fire Brigade attended one of these roughly every other day last year. The fatalities are rising. The injuries are horrific, and they fall disproportionately on delivery riders living in shared accommodation, who buy the cheapest available battery because their margins are non-existent, and who charge it where they sleep.

So what is to be done? Three things. First, the online marketplaces must be brought within the product safety regime as sellers, not as neutral platforms, because that is where the substandard cells and the universal chargers are coming from. Second, we need a mandatory standard for e-bike and e-scooter batteries and conversion kits, with third-party certification, not self-declaration. Third, we need safe charging provision, and that means working with local authorities and social landlords on external charging points rather than simply banning the bikes from buildings, which pushes the risk out of sight without reducing it.

None of that is technically difficult. It requires only that we act before the next inquest rather than after it.

The pattern is what concerns me more than any single episode. The documents that arrive redacted. The committee studies that end when the chair rules a line of questioning out of order. The prorogation that lands in the middle of a study. The undertaking to provide material by a date that passes without comment. Each of these can be defended in isolation, and each is defended in isolation, usually with the observation that previous governments did similar things, which is true and is not a justification.

Will the government commit today to waiving cabinet confidence over the SNC-Lavalin material for any future examination by an officer of Parliament? If the answer is no, then the words we have heard this afternoon about transparency have no content.

Let me give the House the position in my own constituency, because the national figures conceal as much as they reveal. There are children waiting more than two years for an initial assessment of speech and language needs. Two years, in the period of a child's life when intervention is most effective and most cheaply delivered. By the time they are seen, the window has closed, the child is behind, the behavioural difficulties that follow from not being able to communicate have set in, and what would have been a course of therapy becomes a lifetime of support. That is not compassion and it is not economy either. It is the most expensive possible way to run a service.

The assessment of need process has become, in practice, a legal exercise. Parents are advised to seek reports privately because they know the public system will not produce one in time. Those who can pay, pay. Those who cannot, wait. We have constructed a two-tier system for the children with the least capacity to advocate for themselves, and we have done it without ever deciding to, which is somehow worse.

What I want from the Minister of State is not sympathy, of which we have had a great deal. I want the therapist vacancy figures by CHO area, I want to know how many of the posts sanctioned in the last three budgets have actually been filled, and I want to know what is being done about the training pipeline, because you cannot recruit from a pool that the State declined to fund a decade ago.

The Government's position appears to be that this is the conduct of international relations and therefore a matter for the Executive under the prerogative. I understand the constitutional theory. But the Committee is not conducting diplomacy in the ordinary sense. It is administering an agreement that operates as domestic law in part of the United Kingdom, and it has the power to add to the body of law applying there. A body with legislative effect that answers to no legislature is an anomaly, whatever its origins.

The minimum I would ask for is this. Publication of the agenda in advance, with sufficient time for the relevant Committees of this House and of the Assembly to take a view. A written statement to Parliament after each meeting setting out what was decided. And an undertaking that no measure adding to the schedule will be agreed without prior notification to this House.

None of that requires renegotiation. None of it constrains the Government's negotiating position. It requires only that Ministers accept that accountability does not stop at the point where a matter becomes technically complex, which is precisely the point at which it becomes most necessary.

I want to ask the Taoiseach three specific questions. First, what is the Government's assessment of the state of play on the level playing field provisions, which we are told remain the principal obstacle? Ireland has a particular interest here that is not identical to the general EU interest, because the divergence that would harm us most is not in subsidy control but in food and agricultural standards, given the integration of our processing sector with the market next door.

Second, on fisheries. The Minister will be aware of the arithmetic. Ireland's fleet stands to lose disproportionately from any redistribution of quota, and there is a widespread view in the coastal communities I represent that we have historically been the currency in which European fisheries settlements are paid. What assurances has the Taoiseach sought that this will not happen again?

Third, on contingency. The Government has published readiness material and run an information campaign. But the businesses I speak to are not confused about the customs formalities, they are unable to afford the working capital that the formalities will require. A haulier facing a deferment account and duty deposits needs credit, not a leaflet. Is there a scheme, is it funded, and when will the details be published?

I would rather be told an uncomfortable truth today than a comfortable one that unravels in December.

Cost rental is genuinely new in this jurisdiction. It is a model in which rents are set to cover the cost of delivering and managing the home over a long horizon rather than by reference to market comparators, which means that the rent is typically at least a quarter below market and, crucially, it stays below market permanently. That last point is the one most often missed. This is not a subsidy that tapers. It is a different tenure, and once a home is in it, it stays in it. Every unit we deliver this year removes a household from the pressures of the private market permanently and adds a stabilising element to the local rental market as a whole.

On affordable purchase, the first homes have now been delivered under the local authority schemes and under the First Home shared equity scheme. I am conscious of the criticism that shared equity risks feeding into prices, and I take it seriously. Agricultural emissions in this country arise overwhelmingly from biological processes: enteric fermentation in ruminant livestock, and nitrous oxide from soils following the application of nitrogen. These are functions of animal numbers, of feed composition and of fertiliser use. They are not, in the main, functions of economic activity in the sense that transport or industrial emissions are. So while there were undoubtedly disruptions to the sector during 2020, in processing capacity, in market access and in the food service channel in particular, the effect on the emissions profile is likely to be considerably smaller than the effect observed in other sectors, and may be within the uncertainty range of the inventory itself.

What we do know is that milk output continued to grow through that period and that the dairy herd did not contract. Fertiliser sales, which are the more responsive variable, moved with price rather than with the pandemic. I would therefore caution the Deputy against expecting the 2020 figures to show a covid effect that can be cleanly separated out.

On the wider point, which I take to be the Deputy's real concern, the pathway required of this sector under the carbon budgets is demanding and I have never suggested otherwise. Meeting it requires the measures set out in the Climate Action Plan to be adopted at scale and not merely piloted: protected urea, lower crude protein in feed, improved economic breeding index, extended grazing, anaerobic digestion, and diversification of land use including forestry and organics.

The honest position is that adoption to date has been uneven, that the schemes have been designed and funded, and that the rate of uptake will determine whether the sector meets its ceiling. I would rather say that plainly than offer the House a projection I cannot stand over.

We have a constitutional order that is, on paper, among the more protective in Europe. We have a superior court willing, on occasion, to strike down legislation. What we do not have is any realistic mechanism by which an ordinary person of ordinary means can invoke any of it. Civil legal aid is means-tested at thresholds that exclude a person on the average industrial wage. It excludes most cases before tribunals. It excludes, entirely, defamation. And the costs rule means that a plaintiff of modest means who loses against a State body or an insurance company faces the loss of their home.

So the practical position is that constitutional litigation in this country is conducted either by the very wealthy, by those with nothing left to lose, or by those fortunate enough to find a practitioner willing to carry the case on their own resources for several years. That last category is small, it is ageing, and I want to acknowledge it, because those solicitors and barristers have done more to give content to the rights in that document than any Government has.

What would change it? Three things. A properly funded civil legal aid scheme with thresholds reviewed annually. A protective costs order regime for cases raising issues of general public importance, which exists in other jurisdictions and works. And multi-party litigation procedure, which the Law Reform Commission recommended in 2005, which every Government since has accepted in principle, and which has still not been enacted eighteen years later.

That last one is the tell. It costs almost nothing and it has not been done, and the reason it has not been done is that the interests it would inconvenience are well represented in the corridors of this building.

Let me set out the reasoning once more. The GMO framework regulates a process rather than an outcome. I mention this not merely out of local pride, though I have plenty of that, but because the castle tells us something about how places acquire and lose their function, and about the responsibility we have for what happens next.

Berkhamsted was significant because of where it sat on the route north from London. When the route changed, the castle declined, and by the sixteenth century it was being quarried for stone to build elsewhere. Then the canal came, and then the railway, and the town became something else entirely: a place from which people travelled to work in London and to which they returned. That is broadly what it remains, and it has done well out of it.

But a commuter town is a particular kind of economy and it has particular vulnerabilities, which the last few years have exposed. When the pattern of travel changes, as it has, the high street that depended on footfall at eight in the morning and six at night finds the rhythm altered. Some of that has been to our advantage: people working from home spend locally. Some has not: the office space above the shops is emptying, and the business rates on it are not being paid by anybody.

What I want to say to the Minister is that the powers we have given local authorities to respond to this are inadequate. Permitted development has converted offices to flats with no obligation to contribute to infrastructure and no minimum space standards worth the name. The high street rental auction powers are welcome but they are cumbersome. And the heritage that draws people to a town like mine, the castle among it, sits with a national body whose maintenance budget has been reduced in real terms every year for a decade.

On the marine shipping question, the court's conclusion was that the board had excluded from the scope of its review the effects of the tanker traffic that the project would generate. That was a defensible reading of the board's own governing statute and it was the position taken in good faith at the time, but the court found it was too narrow, and having read the judgment I think the court was right. The consequences of a project include the shipping it causes. On consultation, the finding was harder and it deserves a fuller answer than the one the government has generally given. The court did not find that we failed to consult. It found that phase three, the stage at which concerns raised by indigenous communities were to be considered and responded to, was conducted as a note-taking exercise. Officials attended, recorded what was said, and had no mandate to accommodate any of it. Consultation in which the consulting party cannot change anything is not consultation, and the court said so in fairly direct terms.

So the process has been redone. Additional Crown representatives with an actual mandate. A longer period. Accommodations that have been agreed and published. Whether that is sufficient is not for me to declare from this seat, and I will not pretend that the communities involved are unanimous, because they are not, and it would be dishonest to suggest otherwise. Some support the project and have equity in it. Some remain opposed and will continue to litigate. Both of those positions are legitimate and both were arrived at through their own governance.

Here is my argument. This crisis has taught us something that we knew in 1940 and forgot somewhere around 1990: that in an emergency, the capacity to make things in your own country is not an inefficiency to be optimised away. It is insurance. We discovered in March that we could not manufacture a surgical gown. We could not produce a reagent. We had ventilator designs and no production line, and the firms that answered the call were, overwhelmingly, engineering companies that had survived on defence and aerospace work.

That capability exists because the Ministry of Defence has, in a rather haphazard way, kept it alive. And it is now under threat, because the procurement policy of the last two decades has been to buy off the shelf from wherever is cheapest, treating each acquisition as a discrete transaction and ignoring the industrial consequence entirely. Every time we do that we save a sum on the contract and lose a supply chain, and the supply chain does not come back, because the apprentices are not trained and the tooling is sold.

I am not arguing for protectionism, and I am not arguing that we should build everything here, which we cannot afford. I am arguing that the appraisal should include the industrial and strategic value, that the social value provisions we have legislated for should actually be applied, and that where a capability is judged sovereign it should be sustained deliberately rather than surviving by accident.

The shipbuilding strategy gestures at this. The refresh needs to do more than gesture, and I hope the Minister will tell us when we may expect it.
